ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: Bian He is the pre-Chan jade-bearer whom the corpus invokes through the uncut-jade story.
EvidenceBody: The name occurs 78 times in 47 allowlisted texts. The Book of Serenity retells the defining event: Bian He found an uncut stone in a valley of Mount Jing, offered it to King Li of Chu, was told it was stone, and had one foot cut off. Chan interviews compress the story into answers such as “white jade without flaw; Bian He has his foot cut off” (白玉無瑕，卞和刖足). A student explicitly adopts the role by telling Touzi Datong, “I bring you the uncut jade and ask you to carve and polish it”; when Touzi Datong refuses it as beam material, the student says, “then Bian He has nowhere to emerge” (卞和無出身處). Yuanwu’s verse names the repeated offering and its cost: “laughable, Bian He presents the jade three times; even if honored, both feet are cut off” (卞和三獻玉，縱榮刖却一雙足). Another verse draws its own comparison: “Mount Jing’s fine jade—why discern it? … Bian He had knowledge; the king of Chu rejected him” (卞和有智楚王嫌). Zen therefore deploys Bian He as the named bearer of unrecognized jade in answers, student self-comparison, verses, and case commentary. These records, not a general literary biography, define the entry.
